summary: Unequal slot hoarding in dedicated pool causing gradual p99 latency surge
description: Issue summary: Customer reports a steady increase in p99 tail latency over a 6-hour window in their dedicated pool. Throughput (tokens/s) dropped ~18% while overall GPU utilization looked normal. Impact: Multiple user-facing endpoints (chat completion) experienced degraded p99 latency and intermittent streaming disconnects for ~5 hours. Environment: Dedicated pool (customer tenant on dedicated capacity) in prod-us-west running mixed short streaming and medium-length generation workloads.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Send high-frequency short streaming requests (avg tokens per request ~45) with 30 concurrent clients from the customer's fleet. 2) Also run background medium-size batched inference jobs (batch sizes 8-12) on same pool. 3) Observe p50/p95/p99 latency over 30-90 minutes; reproduce on customer's dedicated pool config (reservation: 4 GPUs, autoscale min=4 max=8).
observed_metrics_and_logs:
- p99 latency increased from ~720ms to ~2.4s over 4 hours.
- Overall GPU util remained ~65-78% but per-process kernel queue depth spiked and then dropped cyclically.
- Serving runtime logs show repeated small-batch kernel launches and frequent KV cache evictions: "kv_cache_eviction_ratio=0.47".
- Scheduler traces show one tenant with a high fraction of small concurrent streams occupying slots: tenant_id=n-docs-42, concurrent_slots=63% of pool.
- Autoscaler did not scale up because aggregate queueing signals did not cross scale-up threshold (short requests kept queues shallow).
hypothesis_and_investigation_notes: Initial hypothesis: unfair slot allocation / slot hoarding by many short-lived streaming requests from a single tenant caused increased serialization overhead and prevented efficient batch formation, leading to elevated p99 while GPU looked 'normal'. Investigation steps: pulled per-tenant slot allocation, kernel occupancy profiles, and batch size distribution from 2026-03-10 02:00-08:00 UTC. Found a heavy skew: one tenant generated 70% of request spikes that were <50 tokens and opened many concurrent streams, causing fragmentation of the GPU batch scheduler and frequent kv-cache churn. Also observed high memcpy overhead from many tiny batches. Checked autoscaler logs: scale decisions were based on queue depth thresholds; short bursts were under the threshold and so not triggering scale-up. Cross-checked with network metrics: no packet loss or TLS errors. Checked node-level telemetry: no thermal or hardware throttling.
workarounds_applied: 1) Temporarily applied per-tenant concurrent-slot cap for NimbleDocs (limit set to 20 concurrent slots). 2) Applied short-term request coalescing at edge (grouped bursts within 150ms window) for that tenant. 3) Increased autoscaler sensitivity for the affected pool to consider request rate + small-batch fraction for scale decisions. Result: p99 dropped back to ~850ms within 35 minutes and throughput recovered to ~95% of baseline.
root_cause: A combination of high-volume short streaming requests from a single tenant (slot hoarding) and autoscaler heuristics that ignored burstiness of tiny streams. The scheduler's batch formation algorithm favored fairness by slot counts which, under many tiny concurrent streams, caused excessive small-batch launches, KV cache evictions, and poor GPU kernel efficiency.
resolution_notes:
- Short term: kept per-tenant concurrent-slot cap in place and retained autoscaler sensitivity change for the pool during business hours for 72 hours. Enabled request coalescing buffer for the tenant.
- Medium term (deployed): merged scheduler patch that biases consolidation of tiny concurrent streams into 'micro-batches' when safe (PR: platform/pull/4218). Also added a new autoscaler signal (small_batch_ratio) and a tenant-level throttling knob in the console. Deployment rolled out to prod-us-west 2026-03-12 14:00 UTC across the dedicated cluster; monitored for 24h.
- Post-deploy: p99 returned to baseline and no further slot-hoarding events observed for NimbleDocs.
follow_up_actions: 1) Engineering: iterate on batcher heuristics to reduce memcpy overhead for tiny batches (owner: Serving Runtime). 2) Product: add per-tenant concurrent slot limit UI and documentation (owner: Console). 3) Support: notify customers on best practices for mixed workloads and recommend request coalescing and rate-limiting patterns. 4) Run a stress test simulating mixed short/medium workloads to validate autoscaler signal changes (owner: SRE).
resolution: Workaround applied + scheduler and autoscaler changes deployed; monitoring indicates stable recovery.
